title: Kent State Shootings: Why the National Guard Fired on Students
dek: In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on student protesters, killing four. Confused orders, outdated tactics, and armed confrontation turned a peaceful protest into bloodshed.
why: This episode reconstructs the full course of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the events, and directly helps understand the social fractures of 1960s-70s America.
who: For viewers interested in 1960s-70s American social movements, militarized policing, or historical conflicts, especially those concerned with abuses of power and civil rights.

points.h: National Guard armed and deployed on campus
points.body: On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen with M1 rifles, bayonets, and tear gas arrived at Kent State University, bivouacking on the football field and guarding the ROTC building. This deployment enraged students, even those not previously involved in protests, who felt the war had come to their doorstep. But students were not particularly afraid, because previously the Guard had handled demonstrations with tear gas or scuffles, never firing live rounds. This time, however, they carried live ammunition.

points.h: Confused orders, governor stoking the fire
points.body: Governor Rhodes's rhetoric was inflammatory, comparing protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the KKK, calling them 'the worst people in America.' But in fact, his order to deploy the Guard was not official until May 5, while troops had arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government, and governor about the Guard's mission: the president believed the assembly had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban was not yet in effect. This confused communication laid the groundwork for the ensuing conflict.

On the evening of May 3, students gathered on the Commons to protest, but local authorities moved the curfew from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as 'changing the rules mid-game' and split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat down in the middle of the main road, blocking traffic and singing 'Give Peace a Chance.' Police and Guardsmen surrounded them, with helicopters overhead. Eventually, the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to force students back to their dorms, leaving at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

At 11 a.m. on May 4, about 2,000 students gathered again on the Commons. Despite no official state of emergency, university officials distributed flyers declaring the assembly illegal. Guard commander General Canterbury insisted the demonstration was illegal, but students still spread word of the rally via loudspeakers. By noon, the rally was mostly peaceful, aside from some vulgar chants. Campus police used loudspeakers to declare the assembly illegal and order dispersal, but their voices were drowned out, and a few rocks were thrown at vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two volleys of tear gas, but they missed, and the wind blew the gas away.

The Guard advanced to clear the area, successfully dispersing most protesters, but a group of 52 advanced too far and got trapped against a fenced-in practice field, where they were pelted with rocks. After 10 minutes, they received orders to withdraw and moved toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned, raised their weapons, and fired a 13-second volley totaling 67 bullets. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away), and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Nine others were wounded, with distances ranging from 60 to 750 feet.

After the shooting, there was a dead silence; students stood frozen. Fourteen-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio knelt over Jeffrey Miller's body and screamed, and 21-year-old photojournalism student John Filo captured the image that would shock the nation. But the conflict was not over: protests spread nationwide, followed by the hard-hat riot and the Jackson State shootings. The program emphasizes that this history bears striking parallels to the present and is worth reflecting on.

They're the worst type of people that we harbor in America.
The National Guard had tear gas, and that was basically it for non-lethals. Less-lethal ammunition like rubber bullets hadn't been widely adopted.
Without warning, a group of 72 guardsmen reach the top of the hill, turn, raise their weapons, and fire a coordinated volley for 13 seconds. 67 rounds crack through the early summer air.
Then, silence. After the gunshots, no one moves, no one speaks. Some students literally stand frozen in place, unsure of what to do.
When we're looking back at the story of what happened at Kent State, it really does shock and honestly deeply, deeply sadden me how much it feels like this could have all taken place in 2026.
